title: Chapter 10: Of Effectual Calling
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson explores the doctrine of effectual calling and regeneration—how God changes human nature to enable belief in Christ. Drawing from Westminster Confession of Faith Chapter 10, the session distinguishes between the general call of the Gospel (offered to all) and the special effectual call (given to the elect), and explains that regeneration must logically precede faith, though both may occur simultaneously in time.

outline.title: General Call vs. Effectual Call
subpoints: The General Call is the freely offered Gospel proclamation to everyone
The Effectual Call is God's special grace drawing the elect to receive salvation
Both calls come through the proclamation of God's Word
The church's duty is to preach the Gospel to all, not to determine who is elect

outline.title: Regeneration: Being Born Again
subpoints: Regeneration means rebirth through the work of the Holy Spirit
God's effectual call changes our nature rather than forcing us against our will
Regeneration includes enlightening the mind to see Christ
Regeneration includes renewing the heart from stone to flesh
Regeneration results in a renewed will willing to come to Christ

outline.title: Passivity in Regeneration, Activity in Justification
subpoints: In regeneration, man is completely passive; God is acting upon the dead sinner
In justification, man is active, believing in Christ
The order: regeneration precedes belief, though they may occur simultaneously
Regeneration may be instantaneous or a process, but belief follows new birth

outline.title: The Reformed View: Regeneration Precedes Faith
subpoints: Reformed theology teaches that new birth must logically precede faith
Arminianism teaches that faith precedes regeneration
1 John 5:1 in Greek perfect tense indicates birth has occurred prior to belief
One cannot believe without first being born again
This distinction matters because justification comes through our faith, but faith itself requires regeneration

outline.title: Regeneration of Infants and the Severely Disabled
subpoints: Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit
All babies dying in infancy go to heaven based on God's covenant promises
The severely disabled can be regenerated by God's supernatural work
Regeneration is always through the work of Christ, though knowledge may be communicated supernaturally
This provides comfort to believing parents who lose children

outline.title: Salvation Only Through Christ and the Gospel
subpoints: No one can be regenerated apart from Christ and the Gospel
Sincerity of faith does not save; the object of faith matters
All humans are sinners; the default direction is hell
God's grace in offering salvation through Christ is merciful, not mean or unfair
The church bears responsibility to proclaim the Gospel globally

transcript:
## Introduction to Soteriology

Over the next 13 weeks, we are studying soteriology in our Sunday school class. Soteriology is the study of salvation—salvation in the broadest sense, from what God did in electing His people in eternity past, all the way to what God is going to do at the return of Christ in resurrecting and glorifying all His people.

We are using the Westminster Confession of Faith to help us understand these doctrines. For those of you who are visiting or haven't been with us for long, this doesn't mean that we believe the Westminster Confession is the Word of God. Our Constitution states that the Westminster Confession can be amended and changed, which we do not believe is true of the Bible. The Confession is a good summary of what the scriptures teach on the subjects it addresses. It is not exhaustive, but it is a great summary of what we are to believe concerning God and what God requires of us in His Word.

We call the Westminster Confession and Catechisms our "subordinate standards." They are subordinated to Scripture—or if you think of it another way, Scripture is the foundation on which the Westminster standards stand. They are the words of men, but we do not despise them. The people who put them together were very wise and knowledgeable, so they serve as excellent guides for our understanding—a good systematic summary of what we are to believe.

## Chapter 10: Of Effectual Calling

Last week, we considered chapter 9, which addressed what the human will is and how it operates in relation to believing in Jesus. Today, we are going to ask our confession to help us understand how God changes our nature so that we can believe in Jesus.

This doctrine has several names: "effectual calling" (the title of the chapter), but also "regeneration," "being born again," "conversion," and "irresistible grace." These are all ways of looking at the same doctrine from different perspectives, and they are all helpful ways of thinking about it.

### Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 10, Paragraph 1

> All those whom God has predestinated unto life, and those only, he is pleased in his appointed and accepted time, effectually to call by his Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone and giving unto them a heart of flesh; renewing their wills; and by his almighty power, determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ. Yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace. This effectual call is God's free and special grace alone, not from anything at all foreseeing in man, who is altogether passive therein, until being quickened and renewed by the Holy Ghost, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it.

### Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 10, Paragraphs 3-4

> Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who worketh when and where and how he pleaseth. So also are all other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word. Others, not elected, although they may be called by the ministry of the Word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet they never truly come unto Christ, and therefore cannot be saved. Much less can men not professing the Christian religion be saved in any other way whatsoever, be they ever so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the laws of that religion which they do profess; and to assert and maintain that they may is very pernicious and to be detested.

## General Call vs. Effectual Call

There is a general call of the Gospel—a call that goes to everyone. Can you think of passages in which God, Jesus, or the apostles generally call everyone to come to Christ?

Jesus says in Matthew 11:28-30:

> Come to me, all you who are tired, and I will give you rest.

John the Baptist and Jesus came preaching, "Repent, for the kingdom of God is at hand." They didn't go around checking who should be called to repentance; it was a general call to everyone.

Isaiah 1:18 contains this classic calling:

> Come, let us reason together. Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be as white as wool.

Isaiah 55:1 says:

> Come, everyone who thirsts.

And the very last thing we read in the Bible, Revelation 22:17, is a general call of the Gospel:

> Come, says the Spirit. Come, says the church.

This is the job of the church and every believer—to call all to come to salvation in Jesus Christ. We are not called to figure out who is elect and who is not. We are simply supposed to call. In that sense, we need to have that door-to-door salesman mentality. Every door is a potential opportunity, and we just go there. We are proclaiming the Gospel to everyone who will hear it.

But there is also a special call given to those whom God has appointed to faith—the elect of God. If you have any doubt that God elects people to salvation, please read Ephesians 1.

The general call goes to everyone, and we are to preach the Gospel to everyone. But there is also this special, effectual call given to the elect. The word "effectual" means something that works, something that has an effect. God effectually, sovereignly draws them to receive the Gospel and come to Christ.

Consider Romans 8:30:

> Whom he predestined, these he also called. Whom he called, these he also justified. Whom he justified, these he also glorified.

The way this is written in the original language, the same group that was predestined was called, the same group that was called was justified. Nobody gets on the bus outside of predestination, and nobody gets off the bus once they are called. It goes all the way to the end. There is a special call that leads to being justified—being declared righteous in the sight of God, being reconciled to God, being in fellowship with God.

This effectual call normally comes through the preaching and hearing of the Word of God. Remember what Paul says in Romans 10:

> How can they believe if they don't hear? How can they hear if nobody preaches? How can somebody preach if we don't send them? But believing comes from hearing the Word of God.

Faith comes from hearing the Word of God. That is how God issues this call—both the general and the effectual call comes from the proclamation of the Word of God.

In 2 Thessalonians 2:13, the apostle Paul says:

> We are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brethren, beloved by the Lord, because God from the beginning chose you for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, to which God called you by our Gospel.

One is called to salvation through the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ, through the ordinary proclamation of the Gospel.

Last week, part of my reading plan was Ezekiel 37—the Valley of the Dry Bones. God asks Ezekiel, "Ezekiel, do you think that something would happen if I had you speak my Word to these dry bones?" And the Scripture says the bones were not just dry, they were very dry. By this point, after 36 chapters, Ezekiel had learned to say, "Lord, whatever you tell me, that is where I stand." And he proclaims the Word of God, and the bones come to life. That is a picture of what happens when we proclaim the Gospel. It is not through some other means, but it is through the general call of the Gospel of Jesus Christ that people who are dead in their sins come to life in Jesus Christ.

## Regeneration: Being Born Again

This brings us to the second term: regeneration. This is talking about the same doctrine as effectual calling.

Regeneration comes from Latin, made of two words: "re," which means "again," and "generation," which means "beginning" or "birth." So regeneration is rebirth or being born again—a term that we are more familiar with.

We can think of it this way: God's effectual call does not bring us to Christ by force against our nature. Rather, it changes our nature. It gives us a new nature, a new birth, so that we can come willingly. No one comes to faith in Christ kicking and screaming. That does not happen because we are born again before we come to faith in Christ.

In John 6:37, the Lord says:

> All that the Father gives me will come to me. They will come to me.

It does not say they will be forced to come, or that they will come against their will. They will come. The one who comes to me, I will by no means cast out.

Also in John 6:44-45, Jesus says:

> No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up at the last day. As it is written in the prophets, 'And they shall all be taught by God.'

In Ephesians 2:1, Paul says to the church—those who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ:

> You were dead in your trespasses and sins. He has made you alive.

This happened. Verse 1 happens before verse 8 in the sequence of Ephesians 2. In verses 1 through 5, it talks about our being dead and how, out of the abundance of His love and grace, God brought us to life—we were born again, regenerated, and heard the call of the Gospel. Then in verse 8, he says:

> You have been saved through faith.

Faith follows that birth, not preceding. We are not born again because we believe. We believe because we have been born of the Spirit of God. This entire change of nature—from being dead to the Gospel to being alive to Christ—is of the grace of God.

According to our confession, which is a very good description of what the scriptures teach, this new birth of regeneration includes several elements.

### Enlightening of the Mind

First, there is an enlightening of the mind. Our minds are now able to see the light of Christ.

In Acts 26, Paul recounts his salvation a second time. In Acts 26:18, Paul says that Christ told him:

> I am calling you to open their eyes in order to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.

This was the ministry that God would use Paul to accomplish—to open the eyes of the Gentiles, to enlighten their eyes to see the light of Christ.

### Renewing and Purifying of the Heart

Another element of regeneration is the renewing and purifying of the nature of the heart, which is a core promise of the New Covenant. What comes before Ezekiel 37? Ezekiel 36.

In Ezekiel 36, God, through the prophet by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, says:

> I will give you a new heart.

Then, how are we going to do that? By proclaiming the Word to that people. And that is how the new heart comes, because Ezekiel 37 comes after Ezekiel 36. See how things work?

In Ezekiel 36:26-27, the Lord says:

> I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes.

See, now because we have been born again with a new heart, the Spirit is within us, and we are able to walk in God's statutes.

### Renewing of the Will

Regeneration results in a renewed will—a will that is now willing to come to faith in Christ. Ezekiel 36:27 says:

> I will cause you to walk in my statutes, and you will keep my judgments and do them.

When God begins this work of regeneration, man is passive, not active. In justification, man is active. We are believing in the Lord Jesus Christ. It is an active belief. But when we are born again, we are completely passive. We are experiencing something happening to us and in us.

Ephesians 2:5 says:

> Even when we were dead in trespasses, He made us alive together with Christ by grace, being saved.

We are dead. Dead people cannot be active or active at all. In a very basic sense, as long as you are warm and moving, you are alive. Dead people are not doing either of those things because they are not doing anything. That is how the Bible describes us, apart from the work of the Spirit in changing us. We are passive in coming back to life or being reborn. And once we are reborn, then we are able to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.

## Faith and Regeneration: The Reformed Position

I want to talk now about how faith, belief in Christ, is related to being born again.

I have said this morning that the relationship is that you are first born again, then you believe. Billy Graham wrote a book called "What You Must Do to Be Born Again." From a biblical perspective, it would be a book filled with blank pages, because you do not do anything to be born again. It is God acting in you in response to the preaching of the Word—God's response to the preaching of the Word, not your response.

What is the relationship of regeneration to faith? Regeneration precedes faith. That is the core doctrine in Reformed theology.

Now, there are people who think that faith precedes regeneration. Historically, they have been called Arminians. I am not talking about the people from the country of Armenia. I am talking about those who hold a particular theological belief that faith precedes regeneration—that God acts in response to our action. We are saying that the Bible actually teaches that we act in response to God's action.

See the difference between the two positions? What people sometimes confuse is that they think being born again is the same as being justified before God, when they talk about being saved and include all parts of salvation in that one act.

We are justified before God in a moment—the moment we believe. To be justified means to be declared righteous in God's sight. Nothing is happening to us. Everything is happening outside of us. That is what justification is.

Regeneration happens before that moment—it is what enables us to have faith. That faith is real. It is our faith. We are justified based on our faith. But that faith comes from our heart being changed by God prior to that moment.

### 1 John 5:1: A Key Text

I would love for you to grab a Bible and turn to 1 John 5:1.

1 John 5:1 (New King James Version):

> Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and everyone who loves Him who begot Him also loves him who is begotten of Him.

1 John 5:1 (English Standard Version):

> Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.

Why is that important? That is actually the most literal translation of that particular passage. "Has been born of God." Everyone who believes has been born of God.

We spend a lot of time on grammar here, and grammar is the path to understanding Christ. Consider the simple grammar here: "He who believes has been born of God." What does that tell you?

What happened first in that sentence? Being born of God, right. It is actually a perfect tense in Greek, which means something happened in the past and it has an effect today. So you are born of God prior to the actual act of believing, and you are still born of God. And because you are born of God, you are able to believe.

This is not an invention from the confession. It is what the scriptures teach. The new birth precedes faith. One cannot believe without having been born again.

The reformed position allows for those passages which put salvation and eternal life after faith—which is what we believe. You first have to believe in order to be saved and have eternal life. But before you can believe, God has to change your heart.

## Regeneration Without Knowledge of Christ

Can somebody be born again without knowledge of Christ? What is the consensus? Can somebody be born again without knowing Jesus? Yes or no? The answer is no. No, never.

I think what we struggle with is this: how can somebody know who does not have the ability to know—like an infant or somebody who has a severe handicap that is not able to process things rationally or take in information the way we do? What God does then is supernaturally give them that knowledge.

No one goes to heaven apart from the grace of God and the work of Jesus Christ. So if a baby who dies in infancy is going to go to heaven, that baby is going to go to heaven because of the work of Christ. God will communicate that work to the baby, and the baby will go to heaven if that is what the Lord purposes.

Our confession is very clear on this. Paragraph 3 says:

> Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who worketh when and where and how he pleaseth.

The historical Reformed and Presbyterian position has been that all babies dying in infancy will go to heaven. That is the position going back to the Hodges and Archibald Alexander at Princeton in the 19th century.

Theologically, I, as a minister of the Gospel and as a shepherd of the church, can come to a parent who is a believer in Jesus Christ with a clear conscience and say, "Your baby is in heaven because of the promises of God to be a God to us and to our children." Covenant theology has very practical implications. If you have a theology that says God has no relationship to the children of believers, then you have no hope to give to a mourning, believing parent who just lost their infant child or had a miscarriage.

But I can come confidently to you and comfort you with the Word of God that your child is in heaven and you will once again see that child at the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Lord can also communicate the knowledge to people who are severely handicapped and not able to take in information the way you can, if God chooses to do so. Remember what 2 Corinthians 4:16 says:

> Though our outer bodies decay, the inner man is being renewed.

How? Through the Word of God. People with severe handicaps may have bodies that are already decayed, but the inner man is being renewed. How can a valley full of dead bones come to life? Through the preaching of the Word. It is not any different than somebody who is not able to process information rationally. They are not any deader than the rest of us in responding to the scriptures. The Spirit can do the work there. So this is a very encouraging teaching that we find here in paragraph 3.

## Salvation Only Through Christ and the Gospel

The last paragraph talks about whether somebody who is not a baby—somebody able to think—can be born again without the Gospel of Jesus Christ. The answer has to be no.

I hope I have made clear that is the answer I want you to give, whether you agree there or not. It does not matter how sincere somebody is in their faith. Remember, it is true that if there is a perfectly innocent man in the South Pacific Island, that man might go to heaven. The problem is there is no such person, because we are all sinners in the sight of God. We are all condemned. The default direction is hell. It is God's grace that changes that to heaven.

God is not being mean or unfair. God is just letting things go as they are supposed to go when somebody never hears the Gospel. The blame should fall on the church for not reaching that person in the South Pacific Island.

What if somebody is really sincere in their Mormon faith? What if somebody is really sincere in their Muslim faith? Again, it does not matter the sincerity of your faith. What matters is the object of your faith. Who do you believe in? That is what matters. Not how sincere you are about it, but who you believe in.

No, there is no salvation outside of Jesus Christ. You cannot be born again by just being really sincere in any other faith besides the Lord Jesus Christ. The Gospel of Jesus Christ is the only means through which God regenerates the sinner and brings them to faith.
